text: The query is written, the answer is real — but how you present it matters almost as much as getting it right. This lesson is about the conversation with the Operations Manager, not more SQL.

The Operations Manager doesn't care about Glue Crawlers or group by clauses. They asked one question and want one clear answer first. So the conversation opens with the result itself: for August, Camp Kitchen sold the most units — eighteen hundred forty-two — but Tents and Shelters actually brought in the most revenue, over one hundred eighty-three thousand dollars, because tents cost far more per unit than a camp stove.

That's genuinely useful, because it means a restocking decision driven by unit volume and one driven by revenue point to two different categories. A simple table, with both leading numbers visually emphasized, shows that nuance at a glance instead of making the Operations Manager scan every row and compare mentally.

Just as important is naming what this result doesn't cover, briefly — not as a disclaimer paragraph, but as one or two honest sentences. This is August 2026 only, a single month, not a seasonal trend. These are raw order lines, with no returns or cancellations backed out — and a handful of canceled high-ticket tent orders could move that revenue number more than the same cancellations would move a cheaper category. And this is a one-time snapshot, not a live dashboard that updates on its own.

None of that is hedging. Naming the real limits of a result, clearly and briefly, is exactly what makes it trustworthy instead of a confident-sounding guess — and it's a habit worth carrying into every data project from here forward.

With the answer delivered honestly, the final lesson wraps up everything this project built, and looks ahead to what changes once a second stakeholder needs this kind of answer not once, but every month.
